title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models

paper.title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations.
However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available.
While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation.
We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models.
The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator.
The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution.
By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning.
The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model.
To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories.
Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 × 16\text{ to }549\times lower inference cost.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent advances in few-step generative modeling have enabled high-quality generation with only one or a few model evaluations ( Song et al., 2023 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) . However, one may need to align the generator toward desired properties in downstream applications, such as human preferences in image and text generation or structural properties in biological design. Despite the growing importance of few-step generators, their reward alignment remains relatively underexplored. Moreover, most of these downstream objectives are available only as scalar values whose gradients cannot be propagated through the generator due to non-differentiable rewards or discretization. Together, these considerations motivate an important problem: how to align few-step generative models without access to reward gradients. A straightforward way is to directly fine-tune the generator using reinforcement learning (RL) methods developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, we find that direct fine-tuning transfers poorly to the few-step regime. As demonstrated in Figure 1 , direct methods either make limited progress or suffer from severe reward over-optimization that degrades sample quality. We hypothesize that directly changing the parameters of a few-step generative model is prone to losing the knowledge encoded during pretraining. A promising alternative is to keep the generator frozen and optimize its input noise at test time ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) . While searching the noise through test-time scaling can effectively improve the target reward without modifying the pretrained generator, the process must be repeated from scratch for every generated sample. This incurs substantial inference cost and sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. Figure 1: Motivation Figure. (a) Reward learning curve of NPO, direct fine-tuning, and trajectory-based noise policy. (b) Generated samples over training for NPO and direct fine-tuning. (c) Comparison with test-time scaling methods. As shown in the figure, NPO achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than baselines while maintaining an inference cost comparable to the pretrained model. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which learns an amortized flow policy over the input noise space of a frozen few-step generator. We use the identity that the problem of sampling from the reward-tilted output distribution can be reduced to sampling from the reward-tilted input noise distribution when the sampling path is deterministic. NPO learns this transformation with a flow policy that transports the standard Gaussian distribution toward the reward-tilted input noise distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, NPO preserves the knowledge in the pretrained model. By amortizing the noise transformation, it moves the cost of test-time search to training. To enable more efficient training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation from sampled noise endpoints instead of using conventional trajectory-based likelihood estimation ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We observe that it drastically improves the sample efficiency of our method, as depicted in Figure 1 . We evaluate NPO across image, language, and protein structure generation tasks, covering a diverse range of one- and few-step generators and reward functions. Compared to direct generator fine-tuning, NPO consistently achieves a better trade-off between improving reward and preserving sample quality and diversity. Relative to test-time noise optimization, NPO achieves comparable or higher rewards with 16 to 549 × 16\text{ to }549\times lower inference cost by learning an amortized policy. In comparison to trajectory-based noise-policy training, NPO reaches the same reward levels with fewer reward evaluations. Together, these results demonstrate that NPO efficiently aligns few-step generative models using only black-box rewards, without sacrificing sample quality or inference efficiency.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Few-step generative models. Recent advances have enabled high-quality generation with only one or a few model evaluations. Consistency models learn trajectory-consistent mappings ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2023a ) , while distillation-based methods compress multi-step generators using objectives such as adversarial training or distribution matching ( Sauer et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2023b ) . Flow-map-based and related approaches learn finite-time transport between noise levels or directly from noise to data ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2026 ) . While these methods substantially reduce sampling cost, aligning them with downstream rewards remains underexplored. Reward alignment of generative models. Generative models can be aligned to downstream objectives by reward backpropagation ( Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) , RL-based policy optimization ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , incorporating rewards during distillation ( Duan et al., 2026 ) , or using variational inference ( Lee et al., 2026c ) . Recent work has also studied alignment of few-step generators through policy optimization for consistency models ( Oertell et al., 2024 ) , sample-based variational inference ( Lee et al., 2026b ) , and flow-map-specific approaches ( Mammadov et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) . Although promising, these approaches either directly modify the pretrained generator, which can lead to reward hacking, or rely on model-specific structures. In contrast, NPO keeps the pretrained generator frozen to preserve sample quality and applies across diverse few-step generators. Initial-noise optimization. For deterministic generators, alignment can alternatively be performed by optimizing the input noise while keeping the generator fixed. Test-time methods optimize the initial noise for each sample using reward gradients ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ) or gradient-free optimization ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , but incur repeated inference-time search. Amortized approaches instead learn reusable noise distributions or policies, including Gaussian noise policies ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Miao et al., 2025 ) , reward-gradient-based transformations ( Eyring et al., 2026 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) , and diffusion-based noise samplers ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ) . NPO similarly amortizes noise-space optimization, while supporting black-box reward evaluations with an expressive flow policy trained using endpoint forward-noising updates to improve sample efficiency.

sections.heading: 3 Problem Setup & Background
sections.text: In this section, we study reward alignment of pretrained few-step generative models. Given a generator and a scalar reward function, our goal is to steer generation toward high-reward outputs without assuming access to reward gradients. We first formalize the desired reward-tilted output distribution and review trajectory-based policy optimization.

While this construction is tractable for stochastic diffusion samplers because their discretized reverse transitions are Gaussian, it does not naturally apply to deterministic ODE and flow-map samplers. Existing approaches therefore resort to surrogate constructions, including introducing additional stochasticity into the sampling process ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , computing likelihoods through divergence estimators ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , and learning auxiliary models for likelihood estimation ( Ai et al., 2026 ) . However, these techniques are prohibitively expensive and unstable ( OuYang et al., 2026 ) , or fundamentally change the sampling process and cause discrepancies between reward alignment and base model pretraining.

We first show that learning the reward-tilted noise distribution is sufficient to realize the reward-tilted output distribution through the frozen generator. Then, we propose an ELBO-based objective that approximates the target noise distribution with the flow policy in the noise space. Figure 2: Overview of NPO. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate NPO across image, language, and protein structure generation, covering diverse one- and few-step generators and reward functions. Our experiments aim to address the following three questions: (1) Does NPO achieve a better reward-quality trade-off than direct generator fine-tuning? (2) Does NPO achieve competitive performance compared to test-time methods at lower inference cost? (3) Does NPO learn an amortized policy faster than trajectory-based approaches? Figure 3: Reward learning curve of NPO and direct fine-tuning baselines on 1-step generation. NPO efficiently learns to generate high-rewarding samples compared to the baselines. Figure 4: Reward-quality trade-off of NPO and direct fine-tuning baselines on SANA-Sprint with 4-step sampling. NPO achieves a better trade-off than the baselines.

sections.heading: 5.1 Text-to-Image Generation
sections.text: We first evaluate NPO on text-to-image generation tasks. For pretrained few-step generators, we use SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) and SANA-Sprint ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , which support one- and four-step image generation. We provide additional experimental details in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Rewards and Metrics. We optimize two target reward functions: the LAION aesthetic predictor ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) and JPEG compressibility ( Black et al., 2024 ) , without using reward gradients. To measure reward over-optimization, we report ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) for semantic fidelity and LPIPS diversity ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for sample diversity. Baselines. We compare NPO against three categories of alignment methods. Implementation details for all baselines are provided in Appendix C . (1) Direct generator fine-tuning. Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) applies policy-gradient updates directly to the generator using stochastic transition likelihoods. FAV-B ( Lee et al., 2026b ) fine-tunes the generator using amortized SVGD with zeroth-order gradient estimation from reward evaluations. (2) Test-time noise optimization. Best-of- N N ( Karthik et al., 2023 ) samples N N candidate noises and selects the highest-reward output. ReNO ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) and ZeNO ( Kim et al., 2026 ) perform gradient-based and gradient-free noise optimization at test-time, respectively. (3) Noise-policy learning. ODS ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ) learns a score model in noise space using a trajectory-balance objective. We additionally implement Noise Flow-GRPO, a variant of our method that instead uses trajectory-based likelihood estimation.

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Results
sections.text: NPO improves reward while preserving sample quality. Figure 3 compares NPO with direct generator fine-tuning under one-step sampling. Across both pretrained generators, NPO consistently improves the target rewards, whereas Flow-GRPO and FAV-B show limited or no improvement. Under four-step sampling, Figure 4 shows that Flow-GRPO improves the target rewards, but ImageReward and LPIPS diversity decrease substantially, indicating severe reward over-optimization. In contrast, NPO improves the target rewards while better preserving semantic fidelity and diversity. By keeping the pretrained generator frozen and aligning in noise space, NPO achieves a more favorable reward-quality trade-off. Additional qualitative results are provided in Section H.1 . NPO preserves fast inference by amortizing test-time search. Section 5.1.2 compares NPO with test-time noise optimization in terms of the inference speed. NPO achieves comparable reward while reducing inference cost approximately 16 16 – 205 × 205\times relative to the test-time baselines. By amortizing test-time search into a reusable flow policy, NPO achieves comparable alignment while preserving the fast inference of few-step generation. sections.heading: 5.2 Language Generation
sections.text: Recent work has begun to explore few-step language generation with continuous-flow models ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026a ) . To this end, we evaluate NPO on alignment of few-step language generation models. Additional experimental details on the language task are provided in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5.2.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We use the progressively distilled four-step variant of ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) as the pretrained generator. We introduce a DeBERTa-v3-large NLI model ( He et al., 2021 ) , which is fine-tuned on MNLI ( Williams et al., 2018 ) , to define the target reward as the entailment probability for the hypothesis “This text is about [topic].”. We steer generation toward two topics, politics and science. To evaluate generation quality beyond the target reward, we report GPT-2 Large perplexity ( Radford et al., 2019 ) for fluency and unigram entropy ( Lee et al., 2026a ) for diversity. We compare against the same baselines as in the image experiments. Note that as the reward is scored on the text only after sampling, the gradient is not straightforwardly available. Figure 6: Reward-quality trade-off of NPO against direct fine-tuning on the topic-steering task. NPO maintains perplexity and entropy comparable to those of the base model while achieving higher reward than the baselines.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 Results
sections.text: NPO improves reward while preserving sample quality. Figure 6 compares NPO with direct fine-tuning methods. The direct fine-tuning baselines achieve only modest improvements in topic reward while degrading generation quality. The simultaneous decrease in both perplexity and unigram entropy indicates degenerate repetition rather than improved fluency, as further illustrated by the qualitative samples in Section H.2 . In contrast, NPO achieves higher topic rewards while keeping both perplexity and unigram entropy close to those of the frozen generator. These results show that NPO achieves a better reward–sample quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. sections.heading: 5.3 Protein Structure Generation
sections.text: Several works have been developed to utilize few-step generative models for protein backbone generation ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Woo et al., 2026 ) . However, protein generative models tend to under-sample β \beta -sheet-rich structures, limiting the diversity of generated secondary structures ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we evaluate NPO on protein structure tasks to promote diverse secondary structures with increased β \beta -sheet content. Additional details are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We study reward alignment of few-step generative models without access to reward gradients. We introduce Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which keeps the pretrained generator frozen and learns an amortized flow policy over its input noise to sample from a reward-tilted noise distribution. NPO further uses ELBO-based likelihood estimation to avoid dependence on trajectory-based objectives. Extensive experiments across image, language, and protein generation confirm that NPO provides an effective way to adapt few-step generators while preserving their sample quality and fast inference. Limitation and future works. Although the noise policy is lightweight, it still requires about 2.2 2.2 - 2.6 × 2.6\times the inference cost of the frozen generator. Distilling the noise policy into a one-step or few-step map could further reduce this overhead to nearly match the speed of the frozen generator.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We use large language models (LLMs) only for two auxiliary tasks: (1) minor polishing of the manuscript text for improving grammar and readability, and (2) limited assistance in code implementation for debugging syntax or refactoring functions. LLMs did not contribute to the research problem formulation, core methodology, or the design of experiments. All critical ideas, methods, and analyses presented in this paper are the original work of the authors.

sections.heading: B.4 Noise Policy Architecture and Training
sections.text: Table 3 lists the architecture and optimization settings of the noise policy. For images, we use a conditional 2D U-Net from diffusers , conditioned on the prompt embedding of the generator’s text encoder through cross-attention. For language and protein backbones, the noise is a one-dimensional sequence without a spatial grid, so we use a DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) whose tokens are the positions of the generator input. The flow time t t enters through a sinusoidal embedding in both architectures. Within each domain, NPO and the noise-policy baselines, Noise Flow-GRPO and ODS, use the same backbone. We draw endpoints z 0 ∼ q ψ z_{0}\sim q_{\psi} by integrating the policy flow from z 1 ∼ q base z_{1}\sim q_{\mathrm{base}} with a Heun solver ( Karras et al., 2022 ) . We train the policy with AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) and set the EMA decay in Algorithm 1 to γ k \gamma_{k} at round k k . The learning rate and λ ref \lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} are specified per domain in Appendices D , E and F , and the batch size in Appendix C . sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation of the Baselines
sections.text: We reimplement all baselines in our experimental framework, using their official implementations as references when available. For ZeNO, whose official implementation is not publicly available, we follow the algorithm of Kim et al. (2026) . Within each domain, all methods share the generator, the reward, and the evaluation protocol. Noise Flow-GRPO and ODS use the noise-policy backbone of NPO ( Table 3 ). sections.heading: Noise Flow-GRPO.
sections.text: Noise Flow-GRPO trains the noise policy with the GRPO objective of Liu et al. (2026) , with the reference flow of Section B.1 as the reference model. During training, it samples the policy flow with a 10 10 -step Euler–Maruyama discretization of an SDE with noise level a = 0.7 a=0.7 , and it clips the importance ratio at ϵ = 1 ​ e- ​ 4 \epsilon=1\text{e-}4 . At evaluation, it samples the policy flow with a 10 10 -step Heun solver. We train with AdamW, ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ( 0 0 for proteins), and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0 1.0 ( 5.0 5.0 for proteins).

sections.heading: Flow-GRPO.
sections.text: Flow-GRPO fine-tunes the generator with the GRPO objective of Liu et al. (2026) , with the frozen generator as the reference model. To obtain transition likelihoods, we add Gaussian noise after each sampling step for multi-step sampling and to the output for one-step sampling. We clip the importance ratio at ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 for images and ϵ = 1 ​ e- ​ 4 \epsilon=1\text{e-}4 otherwise. At evaluation, the generator samples without the added noise. We train with AdamW, ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0 1.0 .

sections.heading: FAV-B.
sections.text: We follow the black-box variant of Lee et al. (2026b) . For each of C C conditions, FAV-B draws K K particles from the fine-tuned generator and K K particles from the frozen generator. It estimates the reward gradient at each particle with an antithetic evolution-strategies estimate over N N random perturbations of scale σ \sigma , which costs K ⁡ ( 2 ​ N + 1 ) K(2N+1) reward calls per condition. It adds β \beta times this gradient to the kernel density estimate of the prior score and regresses the LoRA onto the particles moved by the resulting velocity. We use K = 8 K=8 and N = 4 N=4 , with C = 4 C=4 and σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 for images, C = 1 C=1 and σ = 0.1 \sigma=0.1 for language, and C = 1 C=1 , N = 16 N=16 , and σ \sigma equal to 0.01 0.01 times the particle scale for proteins. The kernel bandwidths follow the median heuristic. We train with AdamW, ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.01 0.01 , and gradient-norm clipping at 2.0 2.0 .

sections.heading: ODS.
sections.text: We follow Venkatraman et al. (2025) and use the noise-policy backbone of NPO as the score network. ODS samples the noise with a 25 25 -step Euler–Maruyama discretization of a cosine variance-preserving SDE, during training and at evaluation. It trains with the relative trajectory balance objective toward q base ​ ( z ) ​ r ​ ( g θ ​ ( z ) ) β q_{\mathrm{base}}(z)\,r(g_{\theta}(z))^{\beta} and sets log ⁡ Z \log Z to the batch mean. Each step draws trajectories from the prior with probability 0.2 0.2 , from a uniform replay buffer of size 10,000 10{,}000 with probability 0.2 0.2 , and from the current policy otherwise. We use log ⁡ ( r + 2 ) \log(r+2) for compressibility and the exponential of the secondary-structure diversity score for proteins so that log ⁡ r \log r is defined. We train with Adam and gradient-norm clipping at 0.1 0.1 .

sections.heading: Test-time baselines.
sections.text: Best-of- N N (BoN), ReNO ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) , and ZeNO ( Kim et al., 2026 ) search the initial noise of each sample at inference time and leave the generator unchanged. For each method, we search as many samples as the evaluation protocol of each domain uses and evaluate them in the same way as the other methods. • BoN draws N N initial noises for each sample and keeps the one with the highest reward. • ReNO optimizes the initial noise by gradient ascent on the reward, which requires a differentiable reward, so we run it only on SD-Turbo with one sampling step under the aesthetic reward. We use the default hyperparameters of Eyring et al. (2024) : SGD with Nesterov momentum 0.9 0.9 , learning rate 5.0 5.0 , gradient-norm clipping at 0.1 0.1 , and a norm regularization weight of 0.01 0.01 . • ZeNO optimizes the initial noise with a zeroth-order estimate of the reward gradient. We use the default hyperparameters of Kim et al. (2026) , β = 0.01 \beta=0.01 , η = 1.5 \eta=1.5 , and N = 16 N=16 perturbations per iteration, in all domains.

sections.heading: Generator.
sections.text: We use two frozen text-to-image generators. SANA-Sprint ( Chen et al., 2025 ) is a distilled 0.6 0.6 B-parameter model that generates 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 images from a 32 × 32 × 32 32\times 32\times 32 latent. We run it at one and four sampling steps with guidance scale 4.5 4.5 . SD-Turbo ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) is an adversarially distilled Stable Diffusion 2.1 model that generates 512 × 512 512\times 512 images from a 4 × 64 × 64 4\times 64\times 64 latent. We run it at one and four sampling steps.

sections.heading: Target rewards.
sections.text: We use two target rewards. The LAION aesthetic predictor ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) is a linear head on a frozen CLIP image embedding ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and maps an image to a scalar aesthetic score. JPEG compressibility ( Black et al., 2024 ) is the negative file size of the image after JPEG encoding.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We measure semantic collapse with ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , a learned reward model of prompt–image alignment that no method optimizes. We measure diversity collapse with LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , the perceptual distance between two images, averaged over all pairs of samples that share a prompt.

sections.heading: D.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate on 45 45 simple-animal prompts ( Black et al., 2024 ) with 16 16 samples per prompt. We score every sample with the target reward and ImageReward and report their means. We compute LPIPS between all pairs of samples that share a prompt and report the mean distance. We run each setting with five seeds and report the mean and standard deviation across seeds.

sections.heading: Generator.
sections.text: We use the progressively distilled four-step ELF model ( Hu et al., 2026 ) trained on OpenWebText. The model is unconditional and generates sequences of 1024 1024 tokens from a 1024 × 512 1024\times 512 continuous latent. We run it with its probability-flow ODE sampler. ELF draws its sampling times at random from a logit-normal distribution. We instead place them at the quantiles of the same distribution, which makes the sampler deterministic given the initial noise.

sections.heading: Target reward.
sections.text: The target reward is the entailment probability of the DeBERTa-v3-large NLI model ( He et al., 2021 ) fine-tuned on MNLI and related NLI corpora ( Williams et al., 2018 ) . The premise is the generated text, and the hypothesis is “This text is about topic .” for topic ∈ { politics , science } \textit{topic}\in\{\text{politics},\text{science}\} .

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We measure fluency with the perplexity of GPT-2 Large ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , the exponentiated mean negative log-likelihood of a generated sequence. We measure diversity with the unigram entropy ( Lee et al., 2026a ) H = − ∑ v p v log p v H=-\sum_{v}p_{v}\log p_{v} of a sample, where p v p_{v} is the frequency of token v v in the sample under the GPT-2 tokenizer.

sections.heading: E.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate on 256 256 samples. We score every sample with the target reward, perplexity, and unigram entropy and report their means. We run each setting with five seeds and report the mean and standard deviation across seeds.

sections.heading: Generator.
sections.text: We use the five-step protein backbone generator of Xie et al. (2025) , distilled from Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) with score identity distillation. We run it at K = 5 K=5 sampling steps and generate backbones of L = 150 L=150 residues. We sample without re-injecting noise between steps, which makes the sampler deterministic given the initial noise.

sections.heading: Target reward.
sections.text: The target reward is the secondary-structure diversity score of Venkatraman et al. (2025) , computed from the proportions of α \alpha -helix, β \beta -sheet, and coil residues in a backbone. We assign the secondary structure with P-SEA ( Labesse et al., 1997 ) from the C α \alpha trace instead of DSSP, which requires backbone atoms that the generator does not produce.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We measure designability with the self-consistency protocol of Geffner et al. (2025) and Xie et al. (2025) . ProteinMPNN ( Dauparas et al., 2022 ) designs eight sequences for each backbone, and ESMFold ( Lin et al., 2023 ) folds each sequence. A backbone is designable when the smallest C α \alpha RMSD between the backbone and a refolded structure is below 2 2 Å, and we report the designable fraction. We measure diversity with the mean TM-score ( Zhang & Skolnick, 2004 ) over all pairs of backbones, computed with TM-align ( Zhang & Skolnick, 2005 ) . A lower value indicates higher diversity.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.21125v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026 Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models Woocheol Shin Affiliation: KAIST Email: woofe@kaist.ac.kr Taeyoung Yun Affiliation: KAIST Email: 99yty@kaist.ac.kr Jiwon Sung Affiliation: Stanford University Email: khg2000v@kaist.ac.kr Hyeongyu Kang Affiliation: KAIST Email: pjmin831@kaist.ac.kr Jeongmin Park Affiliation: KAIST Email: jaewoo@kaist.ac.kr Jaewoo Lee Affiliation: KAIST Affiliation: MongooseAI Email: dyun0317@kaist.ac.kr Kyuil Sim Affiliation: KAIST Email: jinkyoo.park@kaist.ac.kr Dohyun Kim Affiliation: KAIST Email: jwsung@stanford.edu Yutong He Email: yutonghe@andrew.cmu.edu Jinkyoo Park Affiliation: KAIST Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Affiliation: Omelet Email: kyuil.sim@kaist.ac.kr Abstract Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 × 16\text{ to }549\times lower inference cost. † † footnotetext: † Co-corresponding authors. Project page: https://shin-woocheol.github.io/npo/ 1 Introduction Recent advances in few-step generative modeling have enabled high-quality generation with only one or a few model evaluations ( Song et al., 2023 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) . However, one may need to align the generator toward desired properties in downstream applications, such as human preferences in image and text generation or structural properties in biological design. Despite the growing importance of few-step generators, their reward alignment remains relatively underexplored. Moreover, most of these downstream objectives are available only as scalar values whose gradients cannot be propagated through the generator due to non-differentiable rewards or discretization. Together, these considerations motivate an important problem: how to align few-step generative models without access to reward gradients. A straightforward way is to directly fine-tune the generator using reinforcement learning (RL) methods developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, we find that direct fine-tuning transfers poorly to the few-step regime. As demonstrated in Figure 1 , direct methods either make limited progress or suffer from severe reward over-optimization that degrades sample quality. We hypothesize that directly changing the parameters of a few-step generative model is prone to losing the knowledge encoded during pretraining. A promising alternative is to keep the generator frozen and optimize its input noise at test time ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) . While searching the noise through test-time scaling can effectively improve the target reward without modifying the pretrained generator, the process must be repeated from scratch for every generated sample. This incurs substantial inference cost and sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. Figure 1: Motivation Figure. (a) Reward learning curve of NPO, direct fine-tuning, and trajectory-based noise policy. (b) Generated samples over training for NPO and direct fine-tuning. (c) Comparison with test-time scaling methods. As shown in the figure, NPO achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than baselines while maintaining an inference cost comparable to the pretrained model. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which learns an amortized flow policy over the input noise space of a frozen few-step generator. We use the identity that the problem of sampling from the reward-tilted output distribution can be reduced to sampling from the reward-tilted input noise distribution when the sampling path is deterministic. NPO learns this transformation with a flow policy that transports the standard Gaussian distribution toward the reward-tilted input noise distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, NPO preserves the knowledge in the pretrained model. By amortizing the noise transformation, it moves the cost of test-time search to training. To enable more efficient training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation from sampled noise endpoints instead of using conventional trajectory-based likelihood estimation ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We observe that it drastically improves the sample efficiency of our method, as depicted in Figure 1 . We evaluate NPO across image, language, and protein structure generation tasks, covering a diverse range of one- and few-step generators and reward functions. Compared to direct generator fine-tuning, NPO consistently achieves a better trade-off between improving reward and preserving sample quality and diversity. Relative to test-time noise optimization, NPO achieves comparable or higher rewards with 16 to 549 × 16\text{ to }549\times lower inference cost by learning an amortized policy. In comparison to trajectory-based noise-policy training, NPO reaches the same reward levels with fewer reward evaluations. Together, these results demonstrate that NPO efficiently aligns few-step generative models using only black-box rewards, without sacrificing sample quality or inference efficiency. 2 Related Work Few-step generative models. Recent advances have enabled high-quality generation with only one or a few model evaluations. Consistency models learn trajectory-consistent mappings ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2024 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2023a ) , while distillation-based methods compress multi-step generators using objectives such as adversarial training or distribution matching ( Sauer et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2023b ) . Flow-map-based and related approaches learn finite-time transport between noise levels or directly from noise to data ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Frans et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ; Boffi et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2026 ) . While these methods substantially reduce sampling cost, aligning them with downstream rewards remains underexplored. Reward alignment of generative models. Generative models can be aligned to downstream objectives by reward backpropagation ( Prabhudesai et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) , RL-based policy optimization ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , incorporating rewards during distillation ( Duan et al., 2026 ) , or using variational inference ( Lee et al., 2026c ) . Recent work has also studied alignment of few-step generators through policy optimization for consistency models ( Oertell et al., 2024 ) , sample-based variational inference ( Lee et al., 2026b ) , and flow-map-specific approaches ( Mammadov et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) . Although promising, these approaches either directly modify the pretrained generator, which can lead to reward hacking, or rely on model-specific structures. In contrast, NPO keeps the pretrained generator frozen to preserve sample quality and applies across diverse few-step generators. Initial-noise optimization. For deterministic generators, alignment can alternatively be performed by optimizing the input noise while keeping the generator fixed. Test-time methods optimize the initial noise for each sample using reward gradients ( Eyring et al., 2024 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ) or gradient-free optimization ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , but incur repeated inference-time search. Amortized approaches instead learn reusable noise distributions or policies, including Gaussian noise policies ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Miao et al., 2025 ) , reward-gradient-based transformations ( Eyring et al., 2026 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) , and diffusion-based noise samplers ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ) . NPO similarly amortizes noise-space optimization, while supporting black-box reward evaluations with an expressive flow policy trained using endpoint forward-noising updates to improve sample efficiency. 3 Problem Setup & Background In this section, we study reward alignment of pretrained few-step generative models. Given a generator and a scalar reward function, our goal is to steer generation toward high-reward outputs without assuming access to reward gradients. We first formalize the desired reward-tilted output distribution and review trajectory-based policy optimization. 3.1 Problem Setup and Reward-Tilted Output Distribution Let g θ g_{\theta} denote a pretrained few-step generator that learns to transport from a source distribution p 1 p_{1} to a target distribution p data = p 0 p_{\mathrm{data}}=p_{0} . Additionally, we have access to a scalar reward r : 𝒳 → ℝ r:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} , which can be evaluated on generated samples but does not need to be differentiable. We provide additional experimental details in Appendix D . 5.1.1 Experimental Setup Rewards and Metrics. We optimize two target reward functions: the LAION aesthetic predictor ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) and JPEG compressibility ( Black et al., 2024 ) , without using reward gradients. To measure reward over-optimization, we report ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) for semantic fidelity and LPIPS diversity ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) for sample diversity. Baselines. We compare NPO against three categories of alignment methods. Implementation details for all baselines are provided in Appendix C . (1) Direct generator fine-tuning. Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) applies policy-gradient updates directly to the generator using stochastic transition likelihoods. FAV-B ( Lee et al., 2026b ) fine-tunes the generator using amortized SVGD with zeroth-order gradient estimation from reward evaluations. (2) Test-time noise optimization. Best-of- N N ( Karthik et al., 2023 ) samples N N candidate noises and selects the highest-reward output. ReNO ( Eyring et al., 2024 ) and ZeNO ( Kim et al., 2026 ) perform gradient-based and gradient-free noise optimization at test-time, respectively. (3) Noise-policy learning. ODS ( Venkatraman et al., 2025 ) learns a score model in noise space using a trajectory-balance objective. We additionally implement Noise Flow-GRPO, a variant of our method that instead uses trajectory-based likelihood estimation. 5.1.2 Results NPO improves reward while preserving sample quality. In contrast, NPO improves the target rewards while better preserving semantic fidelity and diversity. NPO achieves higher target reward under the same reward-evaluation budget, consistently demonstrating that ELBO-based training improves sample efficiency. 6 Conclusion We study reward alignment of few-step generative models without access to reward gradients. We introduce Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which keeps the pretrained generator frozen and learns an amortized flow policy over its input noise to sample from a reward-tilted noise distribution. NPO further uses ELBO-based likelihood estimation to avoid dependence on trajectory-based objectives. Extensive experiments across image, language, and protein generation confirm that NPO provides an effective way to adapt few-step generators while preserving their sample quality and fast inference. Limitation and future works. Although the noise policy is lightweight, it still requires about 2.2 2.2 - 2.6 × 2.6\times the inference cost of the frozen generator. Distilling the noise policy into a one-step or few-step map could further reduce this overhead to nearly match the speed of the frozen generator.
